title: Against Mount Seir: Edom's Old Hatred Judged
summary: Ezekiel prophesies against Mount Seir, the homeland of Edom, for its ancient hatred of Israel. Edom handed Israelites over to the sword in Jerusalem's disaster, gloated over the ruined land, and planned to take the territory of Israel and Judah for itself, forgetting that the LORD was there. God will repay Edom in kind and make it a perpetual desolation.
story: An oracle against a nation seems out of place in the middle of the restoration promises of chapters 33 to 39, since the oracles against the nations ended in chapter 32. It is here on purpose. Chapter 35 is the first half of a pair: Mount Seir is condemned so that the mountains of Israel can be addressed with hope in 36:1-15. Before the land can be restored, the question of who owns it must be settled. Edom claimed it; God answers that the land is his and that he was present there even in its ruin. Edom stands as the representative of every neighbor that exploited Judah's fall, and its judgment clears the ground for Israel's return.
historical:
Edom lay south and southeast of the Dead Sea, in the rugged highlands called Seir. Israel traced the Edomites to Esau, Jacob's brother (Genesis 36), so the hatred of verse 5 is a family feud centuries old. Relations were hostile for much of the monarchy: David conquered Edom, Edom revolted under Jehoram (2 Kings 8:20-22), and the two peoples fought repeatedly.

When Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC, Edom sided with the conqueror and took advantage of Judah's collapse. Several biblical texts remember this bitterly: Psalm 137:7 recalls the Edomites crying to raze the city, Obadiah condemns Edom for standing aloof and cutting down fugitives, and Lamentations 4:21-22 pronounces judgment on the daughter of Edom. Hebrew letters from the fortress of Arad, from Judah's last years, show concern about an Edomite threat in the south. In the following period Edomites moved into southern Judah, a region later called Idumea, while their old homeland declined and was eventually taken over by Arab peoples, including the Nabataeans.
cultural:
Mountains in the ancient world were not only geography but identity. A people's mountain homeland was their inheritance, often associated with their god. By addressing "Mount Seir" rather than Edom's king, the oracle treats the land itself as the defendant, and it prepares for the direct address to "the mountains of Israel" in the next chapter. Verse 10 shows what was at stake: the "two nations and countries" are Israel and Judah, the old northern and southern kingdoms. With both empty of their people, Edom assumed that the land was free for the taking.

The oracle also reflects a principle common in Israel's law and prophets, that punishment should correspond to the crime. Edom did not hate bloodshed, so bloodshed will pursue it (verse 6); Edom rejoiced over Israel's desolation, so it will be made desolate (verse 15). The phrase "even though the LORD was there" (verse 10) captures Israel's conviction that a land belonged to its God, and that the God of Israel had not abandoned his claim even when his people were driven out.
literary: The chapter is a classic oracle against a nation, built in four sections. Each has a charge (introduced by "because"), a sentence ("therefore"), and the refrain "then you will know that I am the LORD" (verses 4, 9, 12, 15). The vocabulary of desolation dominates: the Hebrew root shamem and its nouns run through the chapter like a drumbeat. Verses 12 and 13 quote Edom's own boasts, a technique Ezekiel uses often, so that the accused condemns itself. The chapter's structure is mirrored by 36:1-15, where the same mountains, the same enemies, and the same language of desolation are turned toward Israel's renewal.

outline.t: Edom's claim to the land and its boasting against God
Desolation for the one who rejoiced at desolation

doctrines.note: God's judgment on Edom fits its sin: "I will treat you according to the anger and jealousy you showed in your hatred against them" (verse 11). Nations are held accountable for how they treat the suffering of others, especially for exploiting a neighbor's disaster.

"I heard it Myself" (verse 13). God hears every contemptuous word spoken against his people and against him. His presence in the land ("the LORD was there", verse 10) outlasts the exile of the people.

The land of Israel was God's gift and remained his, even when Israel lost it. Edom's attempt to seize it collided with God's own claim, which is why this oracle opens the way for the promise of restoration to the mountains of Israel.

words.note: Eybah, enmity. A settled hostility, the word used in Genesis 3:15 for the enmity between the serpent and the woman. Here it is called ancient or perpetual hatred, a grudge nursed across generations.
Shemamah, desolation, waste. Six times in the chapter. The word describes land emptied of people and life. Edom wanted Israel's desolation for its own gain; it will receive desolation instead.

Seir, the mountainous region that was Edom's homeland. The name is associated with Esau in Genesis (Genesis 32:3; 36:8). Addressing the mountain sets up the contrast with the mountains of Israel in chapter 36.

christ: The connection here is thematic. The chapter insists that God sees the cruelty done to the defenseless and will repay it, which is why his people can leave vengeance to him. Paul draws on that same conviction when he tells believers not to avenge themselves but to leave room for God's wrath, and to overcome evil with good (Romans 12:17-21). Jesus goes further than the prophets: he calls his followers to love their enemies and pray for those who persecute them (Matthew 5:43-48). That command doesn't deny the justice this chapter announces; it rests on it, since only people who trust God to judge rightly can afford to love the enemy. The phrase "the LORD was there" also anticipates the name of the city at the end of the book, The LORD is there (48:35), and the New Testament hope of God dwelling with his people.

hard.q: Isn't it troubling to celebrate the destruction of a whole people, and are Edom's descendants still under this curse?
hard.a: The oracle is severe, and readers should feel its weight. Several things help place it. It is a judgment on specific conduct, namely Edom's part in the killing and plundering of Judeans after 587 or 586 BC, not a statement about Edomites as a race. Biblical law itself commanded Israel not to despise an Edomite, because he is your brother (Deuteronomy 23:7), and the prophets could imagine Edom among the nations called by God's name (Amos 9:12). The perpetual desolation of verse 9 concerns the land and state of Edom, which did in time cease to exist as a kingdom; the Edomites who moved into southern Judah were later absorbed into the Jewish people under the Hasmonean rulers in the second century BC. The Bible does not teach an ongoing curse on any modern people descended from them. Some readers also take Edom, here and in later Jewish writing, as a representative type of the hostile nations generally.

questions: Edom's hatred was ancient, passed down for generations. How do old family or national grudges shape people who never chose them?
Edom rejoiced over Israel's desolation (verse 15). Why is taking pleasure in someone else's disaster so serious in God's eyes?
What difference does it make to believe that God hears every contemptuous word (verse 13), both those spoken against you and those you speak?
